newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Envoy could serve sentence in Georgia -Shevardnadze.
newsitem.headline: Envoy could serve sentence in Georgia -Shevardnadze.

text.p: A Georgian diplomat expected to face trial in the United States for allegedly causing a crash in which a girl died might be able to serve any punishment in Georgia, President Eduard Shevardnadze said on Monday.

The U.S. State Department said on Saturday that Georgia had agreed to lift immunity for Gueorgui Makharadze, the number two diplomat at its embassy in Washington. The Georgian Foreign Ministry confirmed this decision on Monday.
Shevardnadze, speaking in his weekly radio interview, said "moral reasons" had convinced him to lift Makharadze's immunity.
"This was not a decision based on emotion or haste. Aside from moral reasons, I also had the highest interests of our state in mind. The future will show this to be justified," Shevardnadze said.
But the former Soviet foreign minister suggested that his government would push to have Makharadze serve any "punishment" in Georgia rather than the United States.

"The crime which Giga (Makharadze) committed of course was not premeditated, but is severely punished both in Georgia and in the States. As regards the place of punishment, there will be serious negotiations," he said.

Police say speed and alcohol may have played a role in the January 4 five-car crash, allegedly triggered when Makharadze, travelling at an estimated 80 miles per hour (129 kph), slammed into a car stopped for a red light at Dupont Circle in the heart of the American capital.

U.S. prosecutors were expected to seek a grand jury indictment charging him with involuntary manslaughter now that Georgia has waived his immunity. The charges carry a maximum penalty of up to 30 years in prison.
The accident killed Joviane Waltrick, 16, a Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland, a Washington suburb.
Newsweek magazine has reported that tests at Georgetown University hospital, taken several hours after the accident, showed that Makharadze, 35, had a blood alcohol level far above the legal level.

In suggesting he might seek a deal on Makharadze, the Georgian leader appeared to want to mute domestic criticism of his decision to lift immunity. Some Georgian Foreign Ministry officials have said they disagree with Shevardnadze's decision.
Several independent Georgian newspapers have lambasted it as a "national disgrace" saying Makharadze had been "sacrificed".

Shevardnadze said he had received a "very worried and sensitive" letter both from the diplomat, who was considered the top rising star in the small, newly independent country's fledgling foreign service, and from the victim's mother.
The U.S. State Department is expected to transmit a formal notification of the waiver to the Justice Department on Tuesday.
Lawyers close to the case said there have been no discussions between prosecutors and Makharadze's attorneys about a possible plea deal.
U.S. Attorney Eric Holder last month wrote to the State Department saying his office believed it had sufficient evidence to prosecute the diplomat if his immunity was waived.
